newsitem.title: USA: U.S. senator warns Lott on Clinton plan for D.C..
newsitem.headline: U.S. senator warns Lott on Clinton plan for D.C..

text.p: A key U.S. Senate panel chairman said Thursday he asked Senate Majority Leader Trent Lott not to include President Clinton's District of Columbia revitalization plan in pending tax legislation.

"I remain strongly opposed to the inclusion of any District of Columbia rescue plan in the tax reconciliation bill currently being considered by the Congress," Sen. Lauch Faircloth, R-N.C., chairman of the Senate Appropriations subcommittee on D.C., said at a hearing.
"I have written to Trent Lott urging him not to include such a plan in the tax bill," Faircloth said, at his panel's first public hearing on fiscal 1998 budget requests for D.C.

The Washington Post reported Thursday that federal budget director Franklin Raines met with Lott July 9 to explore ways to get quick congressional action on Clinton's proposed multi-billion-dollar, five-year relief package for the city.
But Faircloth said the President's plan would "greatly reduce" Congress' oversight of D.C., without solving the management problems that plague it.

"A plan which shifts the responsibility for several billion dollars of city services and debts back to the American taxpayer should not be buried in an omnibus tax bill," Faircloth said. "The Senate deserves an opportunity to debate this plan."

A joint House and Senate committee is scheduled to begin work July 11 on the tax portion of a broad U.S. budget bill. Backers of Clinton's D.C. plan are expected to offer a version of the revitalization plan as an amendment to the budget bill.

Faircloth said no amount of "cost-shifting reforms" will solve D.C.'s money problems, which stem from waste and misuse of funds. He added, though, that Congress will not "abandon" its committment to revitalize D.C.

The District and its five-member control board have sent separate $5.17 billion fiscal 1998 D.C. spending plans to Capitol Hill because they could not reach consensus on funding for public safety, corrections and public schools.

D.C. control board chief Andrew Brimmer urged Faircloth's panel to approve the board's plan, while D.C. Mayor Marion Barry and D.C. Council acting chair Linda Cropp endorsed the city's package. Both plans are designed to balance the city's buget in fiscal 1998.
